problem: The error criterion in Q8 is set at a change of one full step Q, but a sampled value is already off by one code when the input moves by half a step, Q/2. The chapter also uses 'aperture time' both for the sampling window and for the error it causes, without separating aperture jitter, so a student can lose marks on the standard half-LSB statement.
fix: Say: if the input moves by more than Q/2 during the aperture window, the sample can be wrong by one code or more. Aperture jitter (variation of that window from sample to sample) is what limits fast-changing inputs; it adds an error ≈ (dV_in/dt) × t_aperture.

problem: The formula is written as exact, yet the sentence just above says 'n clocks plus a little overhead' and Quiz Q4 itself adds one overhead clock. A student who uses T_conv = n T_clk in Q4 gets 6.0 µs instead of 6.5 µs. The formula also ignores the acquisition (track) time, which the chapter has already introduced in Section 1.
fix: Write T_conv ≈ n T_clk + overhead, and f_s,max = 1/(T_conv + T_acq). Say plainly that the n T_clk estimate is a lower bound and real parts add one or two clocks plus acquisition time.

problem: The table has no column headers, so a reader on a phone sees '2ⁿ / fast / 8b' without knowing which cell is comparator count, speed or resolution. The resolution column also mixes units: 8b, 16b and 24b are bits, while the dual-slope entry 4½ is a digit count (about 15 bits).
fix: Add headers 'Comparators | Speed | Typical resolution' and write the dual-slope cell as '4½ digits (≈15 bits)' so all three resolutions can be compared in the same unit.
